A photograph circulating widely on social media shows Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal placing a protective face mask on a young boy, while Deputy Chief Minister Manish Sisodia stands nearby. The image has sparked discussion and criticism, with several users pointing out that both leaders appear to be unmasked themselves while participating in a public health gesture.

To assess the authenticity and implications of this claim, it is important to examine the context in which the image was taken, the background of mask-wearing protocols in Delhi, and the chronology of events surrounding the photo.

Arvind Kejriwal and Manish Sisodia have been prominent faces in Delhi’s efforts to curb the spread of COVID-19. Throughout the pandemic, both leaders emphasized the importance of mask-wearing and social distancing, launching several campaigns to educate citizens about these measures. Among these initiatives, the "Mask Up Delhi" campaign encouraged residents to wear masks in public spaces and distributed free masks to vulnerable populations.

The image in question appears to be from one such event, likely held at a public venue with media presence. In the photograph, Kejriwal is seen bending down to help a young boy put on a mask, a gesture intended to reinforce mask usage among children and families. Sisodia stands beside him, overseeing the proceedings. However, both Kejriwal and Sisodia are not wearing masks at the moment the photo was taken.

This has led to criticism and accusations of hypocrisy, with social media users highlighting the apparent contradiction between the leaders’ public messaging and their actions. The core claim is that while advocating for mask usage, and physically ensuring a child is masked, Kejriwal and Sisodia themselves are unmasked.

To verify this claim, a close inspection of the available images and videos from the event is necessary. Multiple photographs from the same sequence show Kejriwal and Sisodia both wearing masks at different points. However, during the specific moment captured—when Kejriwal helps the boy put on a mask—both leaders have indeed removed their masks. Such removal is not uncommon during speeches, media interactions, or when being photographed, although it does run counter to best practices, especially in close proximity to others.

It is also relevant to consider that public figures may briefly remove masks for clarity while speaking or during ceremonial gestures, such as putting a mask on someone else. Nonetheless, public health guidelines recommend maintaining mask usage in gatherings, particularly indoors or in crowded spaces, regardless of the reason.

In summary, the social media post accurately represents the situation depicted in the viral image. Both Arvind Kejriwal and Manish Sisodia are unmasked while putting a mask on a child, despite their advocacy for mask adherence. While they may have worn masks at other times during the event, the moment in question does show a lapse in personal adherence to the protocol. This incident highlights the importance of consistent public health messaging, especially from leaders, and serves as a reminder that actions must align with the guidance provided to the public.

A widely circulated social media post claims that scientists at the University of Queensland, Australia, have proven that bananas can prevent coronavirus infection by boosting immunity, specifically attributing this effect to the fruit’s vitamin B6 content. This assertion has garnered attention, as many individuals seek accessible ways to protect themselves from COVID-19. However, a closer examination of the scientific evidence and the details of this claim reveals a different story.

First, it is important to understand the context of nutritional science and COVID-19 prevention. Since the onset of the pandemic, researchers worldwide have explored the potential of various foods and nutrients to support the immune system and reduce the risk of viral infections. Bananas are a popular fruit, known for their content of vitamins such as vitamin B6, vitamin C, and minerals like potassium. Vitamin B6, in particular, plays a role in supporting immune function, as it is involved in the production of antibodies and the maintenance of lymphoid organs. However, the link between consuming vitamin B6 and preventing specific infectious diseases, such as those caused by coronaviruses, is far more complex.

The core claim of the social media post is that research from the University of Queensland has proven bananas prevent coronavirus infection. Fact-checking this claim requires investigating several components: the existence of such research, its conclusions, and the scientific understanding of how vitamin B6 and bananas relate to immunity and COVID-19 prevention.

A review of official communications, published research, and statements from the University of Queensland reveals no evidence that scientists there have conducted or published studies concluding that bananas, or their vitamin B6 content, directly prevent coronavirus infection. While the university has contributed significant research to the understanding of COVID-19, including vaccine development and virology, there are no official endorsements or findings supporting the idea that eating bananas provides immunity against coronavirus.

Moreover, while a healthy immune system is essential to ward off infections, no single food or vitamin can "prevent" COVID-19. Vitamin B6, though important for general immune health, has not been shown in clinical trials or laboratory research to offer specific protection against coronavirus infection. The immune system is influenced by a combination of factors, including overall diet quality, lifestyle, age, and underlying health conditions. Public health authorities recommend vaccination, hand hygiene, mask-wearing, and physical distancing as the proven methods to reduce COVID-19 risk.

In summary, the claim that University of Queensland scientists have proven bananas prevent coronavirus through vitamin B6 is not supported by scientific evidence or university research. While bananas are nutritious and can contribute to a healthy diet, they should not be relied upon as a method of preventing COVID-19. Misinformation about food-based "cures" or "preventions" can distract from evidence-based health measures vital to controlling the pandemic.

A recent article published by the Madison Area Lyme Support Group has circulated widely on social media, claiming that COVID-19 was “planned and with purpose.” The article lists a variety of points meant to support this assertion, ranging from the timing of the pandemic to the actions taken by governments and organizations. Given the seriousness of the claims and their potential to influence public understanding of the pandemic, it is essential to examine them through a rigorous fact-checking lens.

First, it is important to set the context. Since the onset of COVID-19 in late 2019, numerous conspiracy theories have emerged, questioning the origins, intent, and responses to the virus. The assertion that the pandemic was “planned” suggests deliberate orchestration, rather than a naturally occurring public health crisis. This narrative has gained traction in some online communities, particularly those skeptical of mainstream scientific consensus and government interventions.

One common claim cited in the article is that the timing of the pandemic aligns suspiciously with various global health preparedness exercises and policy changes. While it is true that global organizations such as the World Health Organization and national governments regularly conduct pandemic preparedness drills, this is standard practice in public health. Preparedness exercises are designed precisely because pandemics are a recognized threat, and such events have occurred throughout history. The existence of planning documents and exercises does not constitute evidence of foreknowledge or intent to release a virus.

Another point raised by the article centers on patents and research related to coronaviruses prior to 2019. While scientific research into coronaviruses has existed for decades, this is due to the fact that coronaviruses are a large family of viruses, some of which have caused previous outbreaks such as SARS in 2003 and MERS in 2012. Patents for vaccines or diagnostic tools reflect ongoing efforts to address known threats, not premeditation for a specific pandemic.

The article also suggests that rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines and coordinated global responses point to prior knowledge. However, the unprecedented speed in vaccine development was largely a result of existing technologies, massive financial investment, and international cooperation. Many of the vaccine platforms had been in development for years, and the urgency of the pandemic accelerated their application.

Finally, the article insinuates that government mandates, lockdowns, and digital tracking measures are evidence of a coordinated plan to control populations. These interventions, however, mirror actions taken during previous pandemics and public health emergencies, where restricting movement and tracing contacts were proven methods to limit disease spread. The adoption of such measures reflects the gravity of the crisis, not a preexisting agenda.

In summary, while the claims presented by the Madison Area Lyme Support Group reflect concerns and skepticism shared by some segments of the public, there is no credible evidence to support the assertion that the COVID-19 pandemic was planned or orchestrated with deliberate purpose. The emergence and global spread of COVID-19 are consistent with patterns observed in other infectious disease outbreaks. Fact-checking reveals that the connections drawn in the article rely on coincidences, misinterpretations, and a misunderstanding of standard public health practices rather than substantiated facts.

A WhatsApp message that has circulated widely since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic claims that, under the Disaster Management Act, only government departments are permitted to post, update, or share any information related to coronavirus. The message further asserts that it is a punishable offence for anyone else to share such information, including forwarding messages about COVID-19.

This claim has caused confusion and concern among social media users, many of whom worry that they could face legal consequences simply for sharing health updates or news articles. To clarify the facts, it is important to examine the Disaster Management Act, how it has been applied during the pandemic, and what these laws actually mean for individuals sharing information.

**Background and Context**

The Disaster Management Act, 2005, is a law enacted by the Indian government to provide for effective management of disasters and related matters. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Act was invoked to allow for coordinated government response and to issue guidelines for public safety.

As misinformation about the coronavirus spread rapidly, the government did issue advisories urging the public to rely on official sources and avoid sharing unverified information. Authorities have also warned that spreading rumors or false information could result in legal action under various laws, including sections of the Indian Penal Code related to public nuisance, or the Information Technology Act.

**Fact-Checking the Claim**

The core claim in the viral WhatsApp message is that "no one apart from government departments is allowed to post, update or share any forward related to Coronavirus" and that doing so is a punishable offence under the Disaster Management Act.

Upon examination, the Disaster Management Act does not contain any provision that categorically bans individuals from sharing information or updates about COVID-19. There is no blanket prohibition on forwarding messages, posting on social media, or discussing the pandemic publicly. The Act empowers authorities to take action against those who deliberately spread false information that can cause panic or disrupt public order. For instance, the law can be used against those who knowingly disseminate fake news, rumors, or misleading information with malicious intent.

However, the Act does not criminalize the sharing of all COVID-related information by private individuals. Official advisories emphasize the importance of verifying information before sharing, but lawful sharing of news articles, government updates, scientific findings, or personal experiences is not an offence. Only the deliberate, malicious, or reckless spread of false information that endangers public safety can attract legal consequences.

**Conclusion**

The claim that only government departments are allowed to share information about coronavirus and that it is a punishable offence for anyone else to do so is false and misleading. The Disaster Management Act does not impose such a blanket ban. Individuals are encouraged to share verified, accurate information and to avoid circulating rumors or unverified claims, but sharing legitimate updates or discussions about COVID-19 is not an offence. The focus of the law is on preventing the spread of harmful misinformation, not on policing all communication about the pandemic.

За да се пројасни фактичното, е важно да се проучи Законот за управување со катастрофи, како што е применет по време на пандемијата, и какви се овие закони за луѓето кои споделуваат информации.

**Позадина и контекст**

Законот за управување со катастрофи, 2005 година, е закон кој го присвојил Индискиот владејуќи правен систем за ефективно управување со катастрофи и поврзани зборови. Кога лажни информации за коронавирусот се ширеле брзо, владата ја издала насоката да ги корисниците на социјални мрежи да се вежуваат на официјални извори и да избегуваат споделување на непотврдени информации. На пример, законот може да се применува на луѓето кои намерно ги споделуваат фалшиви вести, фалшиви информации или заблуди со злобно намера.

Од друга страна, законот не преступно го забранува споделувањето на сите информации поврзани со КОВИД-19 од страна на приватни лица. Само намерното, злобно или непосветено ширење на лажни информации која ја угрожува јавната безбедност може да доведе до јавна одговорност.

**Заклучок**

Тврдењето дека само владини одделенија се дозволено да споделуваат информации за коронавирусот и дека е преступно за секоја друга личност да го стори тоа е лажно и оштетително. Фокусот на законот е да се предотврати ширењето на штетни лажни информации, а не да се контролира сите комуникација за пандемијата.

As India grapples with a significant surge in COVID-19 cases, an image has been widely circulated across social media platforms, drawing intense emotional reactions and raising concerns about the country’s healthcare infrastructure. The photograph in question shows a woman sitting on a road, clutching an oxygen cylinder, with several vehicles parked around her. The image is often shared with a caption stating, “This is where India is right now,” suggesting that the scene is representative of the current situation facing many Indians during the pandemic’s second wave.

To assess the veracity of this claim, it is essential to examine both the authenticity of the image and the context in which it was taken.

Background and Context

India experienced a dramatic spike in COVID-19 cases during the second wave in early 2021, with daily case counts surpassing 300,000 and reports of overwhelmed hospitals, acute shortages of medical oxygen, and desperate patients and families seeking care. Images and stories of patients waiting outside hospitals, makeshift COVID-19 care centers, and people searching for oxygen cylinders became common in news reports and social media updates.

Fact-Checking the Claim

A reverse image search confirms that the photograph is real and not digitally altered. Multiple reputable news outlets published similar images during the height of the crisis. The specific image in question was reportedly taken in Delhi, one of the cities hardest hit during the surge. According to news reports and eyewitness accounts, the woman was waiting outside a hospital, hoping to secure admission or medical attention for herself or a loved one, while using an oxygen cylinder to alleviate severe respiratory distress.

These circumstances were not isolated. During the peak of the COVID-19 case surge, many hospitals in major Indian cities reported being at full capacity, forcing patients to wait outside in ambulances, private vehicles, or even on the pavement, often with their own oxygen supplies. Social media and news outlets documented numerous such instances, highlighting the severity of the oxygen shortage and the strain on healthcare resources.

Analysis

The viral image does not depict a staged or fabricated scene. Instead, it captures a moment that, while heartbreaking, accurately reflects the dire situation faced by many Indians during the COVID-19 crisis. The photograph serves as a stark representation of the challenges faced by patients and their families amid unprecedented demand for medical resources.

However, it is important to note that while this image is authentic, India is a large and diverse country, and experiences varied across different regions and communities. Not every hospital or locality faced identical shortages or conditions. Nevertheless, the image is emblematic of the broader systemic challenges experienced during the pandemic’s second wave.

Conclusion

The social media post’s core claim—that the image of a woman sitting on a road with an oxygen cylinder illustrates the current crisis in India—is accurate in representing the gravity of the situation during the COVID-19 surge. The photograph is authentic and reflects real events that occurred in several locations across the country. It symbolizes the struggles faced by many Indians seeking medical care during one of the nation’s most challenging public health emergencies.

As India faces a surge in active COVID-19 cases, social media platforms and messaging apps have become inundated with messages claiming to provide urgent support for those affected. One such message, widely circulating on WhatsApp, begins with “Anyone requiring Plasma for Covid treatment” and includes a list of approximately 29 alleged plasma donor names and their contact numbers. This message has raised both hope and questions among recipients, prompting the need for thorough fact-checking.

**Background and Context**

During previous waves of the COVID-19 pandemic, plasma therapy—using plasma from recovered patients to treat those currently infected—gained traction as a potential treatment. Hospitals and medical professionals, especially in 2020 and early 2021, called for plasma donations to help critically ill patients. As the demand grew, so did the spread of messages on social media, often containing lists of alleged donors and their contact details.

However, medical understanding of plasma therapy has evolved. By mid-2021, health authorities in India and globally, including the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the World Health Organization, concluded that plasma therapy was not effective in treating COVID-19 and removed it from official treatment protocols. Despite this, similar donor lists have repeatedly surfaced, especially during times of crisis, leading to confusion and, at times, exploitation.

**Fact-Checking the Viral WhatsApp Message**

Upon close examination, there are several red flags associated with the viral WhatsApp message offering plasma donors:

1. **Recycled Content**: The same or similar lists have been circulated during earlier waves of the pandemic, often with identical names and numbers. Many recipients who tried contacting the numbers reported they were unreachable, incorrect, or belonged to individuals unaware of any such initiative.

2. **Lack of Verification**: There is no evidence that the individuals listed are verified donors or have agreed to have their personal information shared publicly. Responsible plasma donation is coordinated through official channels—such as registered blood banks or hospitals—where donor eligibility is medically assessed.

3. **Potential for Misinformation and Harassment**: Sharing unverified contact information exposes individuals to potential privacy violations and harassment. Several people named in these lists have previously complained about receiving incessant calls for plasma requests, despite having no involvement.

4. **Obsolescence of Plasma Therapy**: Major health authorities no longer recommend plasma therapy for COVID-19 treatment. Hospitals have shifted focus to other evidence-based treatments, and plasma donation drives for COVID-19 are largely discontinued.

5. **Risk of Scams**: In the past, similar messages have been linked to scams, where fraudsters pretend to be donors and demand payment for plasma donations, exploiting desperate families.

**Conclusion**

The WhatsApp message circulating with the claim “Anyone requiring Plasma for Covid treatment” and a list of donor names and numbers is not based on current medical guidelines and is most likely recycled or fabricated. The practice of sharing such unverified lists is not only ineffective but also potentially harmful. Those seeking help for COVID-19 should consult qualified healthcare providers or government-approved helplines and avoid relying on unverified social media messages. The spread of such information highlights the ongoing need for vigilance and responsible sharing of health-related content, especially during public health emergencies.

Durante le precedenti onde della pandemia di COVID-19, la terapia con plasma – che utilizza il plasma di pazienti recuperati per trattare quelli attualmente infetti – ha guadagnato popolarità come potenziale trattamento. Ospedali e professionisti medici, specialmente nel 2020 e all'inizio del 2021, hanno chiesto donazioni di plasma per aiutare i pazienti gravi. A metà del 2021, autorità sanitarie in India e a livello globale, tra cui il Consiglio Indiano per la Ricerca Medica (ICMR) e l'Organizzazione Mondiale della Sanità (OMS), hanno concluso che la terapia con plasma non era efficace per il trattamento del COVID-19 e l'ha rimossa dai protocolli ufficiali di trattamento. Nonostante ciò, elenchi simili di donatori sono emersi ripetutamente, soprattutto durante periodi di crisi, causando confusione e, in alcuni casi, abuso.

Analizzando in dettaglio, ci sono diversi segnali di allarme associati al messaggio virale su WhatsApp che offre donatori di plasma:

Molti destinatari che hanno provato a contattare i numeri hanno segnalato che non erano raggiungibili, erano errati o appartenevano a persone non a conoscenza di alcuna iniziativa simile.

A recent social media post has circulated alarming claims about COVID-19 vaccination and menstruation, advising women not to take the vaccine five days before or after their periods. The post suggests that immunity is significantly lowered during menstruation and that the vaccine further decreases immunity before eventually building it up, thereby increasing the risk of illness if vaccinated around one’s period. These assertions have sparked concern and confusion among women considering vaccination. This article examines the facts behind these claims and provides accurate, science-based information.

At the heart of the post is the claim that menstruation weakens a woman’s immune system, making her more vulnerable to infections. It goes on to say that vaccination temporarily reduces immunity, suggesting a compounded risk if vaccination and menstruation coincide. These statements are not supported by scientific evidence.

First, menstruation is a natural biological process involving the shedding of the uterine lining. While hormonal changes do occur during the menstrual cycle, research does not show that women experience a significant drop in immunity during their periods. The immune system is complex and influenced by many factors, but menstruation itself does not cause immunosuppression. Most women are able to go about their daily activities, including attending work or school, during their periods without increased susceptibility to illness.

Second, the function of vaccines, including COVID-19 vaccines, is to train the immune system to recognize and fight specific pathogens. After vaccination, the immune system mounts a response, which can cause mild side effects like fever or fatigue—signs the body is building immunity. There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines, or other routine vaccines, cause a period of decreased immunity that would put recipients at higher risk for infection. On the contrary, vaccination is designed to strengthen the body’s defenses.

Health authorities worldwide, including leading organizations, recommend COVID-19 vaccination for everyone eligible, regardless of where they are in their menstrual cycle. There is no medical or scientific reason to avoid vaccination before, during, or after your period. Vaccines have been tested in large, diverse populations, including women of childbearing age, and no increased risk has been observed related to the timing of vaccination and menstruation.

It is true that some women have reported temporary changes in their menstrual cycle following vaccination, such as lighter or heavier bleeding, or a slightly earlier or later period. However, these changes have been found to be short-term, and there is no evidence that they indicate a compromised immune response or increased health risk.

Spreading misinformation about vaccination and menstruation can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and unnecessary anxiety. It is important to rely on trusted medical guidance. If you have specific health concerns regarding vaccination and your menstrual cycle, consult a healthcare provider. There is no need to delay or reschedule vaccination based on your period. Vaccination remains the safest and most effective way to protect yourself and others against serious illness.

Om du har specifika hälsoproblem angående vaccination och din menstruationscykel, konsultera en vårdgivare. As India grappled with a devastating second wave of COVID-19 in 2021, social media platforms, particularly Twitter, became inundated with posts and videos allegedly depicting the crisis's grim realities. One widely circulated video purportedly showed people collapsing on the streets, with claims suggesting these incidents were a direct result of COVID-19 infections overwhelming the Indian population. The video has sparked fear, outrage, and widespread discussion online. However, a closer examination reveals that the video may not depict what it claims.

**Background and Context**

India’s second wave of COVID-19, which surged in April and May 2021, was marked by soaring infection rates, severe shortages of medical supplies, and heartbreaking scenes outside hospitals and crematoriums. Social media became a crucial platform for sharing real-time updates, requesting medical assistance, and highlighting the crisis. However, the urgency and chaos also gave rise to the rapid dissemination of misinformation and unverified content.

**Examining the Viral Video**

The video in question shows several individuals suddenly collapsing on roads, sidewalks, or in public spaces. Twitter users have widely shared it, often accompanied by captions or commentary linking the collapses to the ongoing COVID-19 crisis in India. The implication is clear: that the severity of the virus was causing people to faint and die on the spot in public areas.

To fact-check this claim, it is essential to analyze the video's origins, content, and context. Upon closer inspection, several inconsistencies emerge. First, the footage does not show any medical personnel, emergency response, or individuals wearing personal protective equipment (PPE), which were common sights in genuine COVID-19 crisis footage from India during the second wave. Additionally, the clothing, vehicles, and signage visible in the video do not always match what would be expected in Indian urban environments.

Reverse image and video searches suggest that the clip was not filmed during India’s second COVID-19 wave. In fact, similar videos have surfaced in previous years from different countries, often in unrelated contexts such as chemical spills or unrelated medical emergencies. In some cases, the same video has been shared in relation to events in China or other countries, long before the 2021 surge in India.

**Analysis and Conclusion**

The veracity of the claim that the video shows people collapsing in India due to COVID-19 during the second wave is highly questionable. There is no credible evidence linking the video to the Indian crisis, nor is there confirmation that the collapses are COVID-related. Health experts have stated that sudden collapse in the street is not a typical presentation of COVID-19 infection, which more commonly causes respiratory symptoms that worsen over days.

This case highlights the importance of verifying the source and context of viral videos before drawing conclusions. While the humanitarian crisis during India’s second wave was real and severe, relying on sensational and unverified footage can distort public understanding and fuel misinformation.

In summary, the video circulating on Twitter does not provide authentic evidence of people collapsing on the road due to COVID-19 during India’s second wave. It serves as a reminder to approach social media content with caution and to rely on verified information to understand complex public health crises.

article_content:
Images circulating on social media have sparked concerns about the authenticity and reliability of COVID-19 test results. The posts claim that the presence of "positive" and "negative" control swabs in COVID-19 test kits serves as evidence that test outcomes are manipulated or predetermined. This article examines the claim, provides background on diagnostic testing protocols, and analyzes the role of control swabs in laboratory settings.

Understanding the Claim

The viral posts typically feature photographs of COVID-19 test kit components, with particular attention to control swabs labeled "positive" and "negative." Users suggest that these controls indicate the test can be made to show any result, fueling suspicions that results are intentionally fixed or unreliable. The implication is that the inclusion of these controls undermines the integrity of COVID-19 testing, potentially affecting public trust in pandemic response measures.

Background on Diagnostic Test Controls

To assess this claim, it is essential to understand the standard procedures in laboratory diagnostics. Control swabs—both positive and negative—are a routine part of test kits used for a wide range of infectious diseases, not just COVID-19. Their primary function is to validate that the test is working as intended.

- **Positive Control Swab:** Contains material that will produce a positive result when the test is functioning correctly. It does not contain live virus but includes synthetic fragments that mimic the target pathogen.
- **Negative Control Swab:** Contains material that should produce a negative result, confirming the absence of the target pathogen.

These controls do not interact directly with patient specimens. Instead, they are used during quality control procedures, often in the manufacturing process or in laboratory settings, to confirm that the testing reagents and equipment are working properly. This ensures that the test can accurately detect the presence or absence of the virus in real patient samples.

Fact-Checking the Manipulation Claim

The assertion that control swabs are proof of manipulated or fixed results is not substantiated by how diagnostic testing works. The controls are not included to alter patient test results. Rather, they are safeguards to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the test. When a new batch of test kits is produced, laboratories use the positive and negative controls to verify that the kits are working as intended before they are used with real samples.

In clinical use, only the patient’s specimen is tested; the control swabs are not introduced into the patient’s test process. If controls are run and produce unexpected results (for example, the negative control shows a positive result), it indicates a problem with the test, and the batch may be rejected or investigated further. This process is a standard part of laboratory science and is essential for maintaining trust in medical diagnostics.

Conclusion

The social media claim misinterprets the purpose of positive and negative control swabs in COVID-19 test kits. The existence of control swabs does not mean that test results are manipulated or predetermined. Instead, these controls are a key part of rigorous quality assurance procedures designed to enhance the reliability of COVID-19 testing. Misunderstanding their role can contribute to misinformation and unnecessary fears regarding public health measures.

Понудување на тврдбата

Вирусните постови обично прикажуваат слики од компонентите на тестови за коронавирус, со посебно внимание на контролни влакна маркирани како "позитивни" и "негативни". Импликацијата е дека вклучувањето на овие контроли подминува интегритетот на тестови за коронавирус, што може да влијае на јавниот доверба кон мерките за одговор на пандемијата.

Позадина за контроли на дијагностички тестови

За да се процени тврдбата, е важно да се разбере стандардните процедури во лабораториска дијагностика. Нивната основна улога е да се потврди дека тестот работи како треба.

- **Позитивен контролен влакен** содржи материјал кој ќе произведе позитивен резултат кога тестот работи како треба. Не содржи жив вирус, но вклучува синтетички фрагменти кои имитираат целата патоген.
- **Негативен контролен влакен** содржи материјал кој треба да произведе негативен резултат, потврдувајќи дека целата патоген не присуствува.

Овие контроли не влезуваат директно во пациенчките узороци. Вместо тоа, се користат во процесите за контрола на квалитет, често во производството или во лабораториски услови, за да се потврди дека тестот и опремата работат како треба. Ова гарантира дека тестот може да точно детектира присуството или одсуството на вирусот во реални пациенчки узороци.

Проверка на тврдбата за манипулација

Тврдбата дека контролни влакна служат како доказ за манипулиран или фиксиран резултат не е доказана од начинот на работа на дијагностичкиот тест. Контролните влакна не се вклучени за да се промени резултатот од пациенчките тестови. Вместо тоа, тие се безбедносни мерења за да се осигури точноста и надежноста на тестот. Кога се произведе нова кутија со тестови, лабораториите ги користат позитивните и негативните контроли за да потврдат дека кутијата работи како треба пред да се користи со реални узороци.

Во клиничка употреба, само пациенчкот узорок се тестира; контролните влакна не се вклучуваат во процесот на пациенчките тестови. Ако контролите се извршени и произведуваат непредвидени резултати (на пример, негативниот контролен влакен покажува позитивен резултат), тоа покажува проблем со тестот, и кутијата може да се откаже или да се направи дополнителна анализа. Овој процес е дел од стандардната лабораториска наука и е важно за да се осигури доверба во медицинската дијагностика.

Заклучок

Тврдбата на социјалните мрежи ги неправилно интерпретира улогата на позитивните и негативните контролни влакна во тестови за коронавирус. Присуството на контролни влакна не значи дека резултатите се манипулирани или предопределени. Вместо тоа, овие контроли се важен дел од строги процеси за контрола на квалитетот, кои се дизајнирани за да подобрат надежноста на тестови за коронавирус. Неправилното разбирање на нивната улога може да допринесе за пропагација на несигурности и непотребни страхи за јавни здравствени мерки.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated stating that the COVID-19 vaccine produced by Bharat Biotech has been approved for children above 12 years. This claim has prompted questions among parents, healthcare professionals, and the general public regarding the current status of COVID-19 vaccination for adolescents in India. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is important to review the background of Bharat Biotech’s vaccine, regulatory decisions, and official guidelines surrounding its use in children.

Bharat Biotech is the manufacturer of Covaxin, one of the two primary COVID-19 vaccines initially deployed in India’s nationwide immunization drive. Covaxin is an inactivated virus vaccine and was initially authorized for use in adults, following rigorous clinical trials and emergency use approval granted by Indian regulatory authorities in early 2021.

With the evolving nature of the pandemic and the need to protect younger age groups, Bharat Biotech conducted additional clinical trials to evaluate the safety and efficacy of Covaxin in children and adolescents. These studies aimed to determine whether the vaccine could be safely administered to individuals under 18 years of age, an essential step before any regulatory approval for use in younger populations.

In late 2021, after reviewing the clinical trial data submitted by Bharat Biotech, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO), India’s national regulatory agency, granted emergency use authorization for Covaxin in children aged 12 to 18 years. This decision was based on the safety profile and immune response data observed during the trials. The announcement was widely covered and marked a significant expansion of India’s vaccination program, allowing adolescents above 12 years to receive Covaxin under medical supervision.

Following this approval, the Indian Ministry of Health incorporated Covaxin into its adolescent immunization strategy. Vaccination for children above 12 years was rolled out in phases, prioritizing those with underlying health conditions and gradually expanding to the general adolescent population. Covaxin became one of the vaccines available for children aged 12 and above, alongside other options such as ZyCoV-D, developed by Zydus Cadila, which was also approved for use in children.

As of 2024, Covaxin remains authorized for use in individuals aged 12 years and older, in line with the regulatory approval previously granted. However, it is worth noting that recommendations and policies may vary over time as new data emerges and additional vaccines are developed. Parents and guardians are advised to consult official government sources or healthcare providers for the most current information regarding eligibility and vaccine availability.

In summary, the core claim presented in the social media post—that the COVID-19 vaccine by Bharat Biotech has been approved for children above 12 years—is accurate. The regulatory approval and subsequent rollout confirm that Covaxin is permitted for use in adolescents aged 12 and above in India. As with all medical interventions, ongoing monitoring and updates to guidelines ensure the continued safety and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccination efforts.

Na koniec 2024 roku Covaxin nadal jest autoryzowany do stosowania u osób powyżej 12. roku życia, zgodnie z wcześniej wydawaną autoryzacją regulacyjną. Warto jednak zauważyć, że zalecenia i polityki mogą się zmieniać w czasie, gdy pojawiają się nowe dane oraz rozwijane są dodatkowe szczepionki. Rodzice i opiekunowie zaleca się konsultację oficjalnych źródeł rządowych lub specjalistów medycznych w celu uzyskania najbardziej aktualnych informacji dotyczących kwalifikacji i dostępności szczepionki.

Autoryzacja regulacyjna i kolejne wprowadzenie szczepionki potwierdzają, że Covaxin jest dopuszczony do stosowania u adolescentów powyżej 12. roku życia w Indiach. Jak w przypadku wszystkich interwencji medycznych, ciągłe monitorowanie i aktualizacje wskazówek gwarantują dalszą bezpieczeństwo i skuteczność działań szczepieniowych przeciwko COVID-19.

A recent social media post claims that “Indians have thrown idols of Gods they worship on the streets since they’ve lost faith.” The statement suggests a widespread loss of religious faith in India, leading to the mass disposal of religious idols. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to consider the cultural, religious, and social context of idol worship in India, as well as the circumstances that lead to the disposal of religious idols.

Idol worship is a central aspect of Hindu religious practice, which is predominant in India. Idols of deities are commonly used in temples, homes, and during religious festivals. Notably, during annual festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi and Durga Puja, idols are created, worshipped for a designated period, and then immersed in water bodies as a ritual marking the conclusion of the festival. This immersion, known as “visarjan,” is a time-honored tradition rooted in religious texts and customs, symbolizing the cyclical nature of life and the transitory presence of the divine in material form.

Occasionally, images and reports emerge, especially after major festivals, showing idols discarded near rivers, lakes, or even on the streets. These incidents are most often a result of logistical challenges, improper planning, or environmental restrictions that prevent proper immersion, rather than a conscious act of disrespect or a loss of faith. In some urban areas where traditional water bodies are inaccessible or polluted, authorities may impose restrictions on idol immersion, leading to temporary accumulation of idols in public spaces until they can be disposed of appropriately.

Moreover, Hindu religious practice mandates that old, broken, or damaged idols should not be worshipped and must be respectfully disposed of. The prescribed methods include immersion in water or burial, but due to lack of proper facilities or awareness, some individuals may leave these idols in public places, inadvertently causing what appears to be disrespect. Social and environmental organizations, as well as local governments, have increasingly advocated for eco-friendly idols and organized collection drives to address the improper disposal of idols.

Contrary to the implication of the social media post, there is no evidence to suggest that a significant portion of the Indian population is discarding idols due to a widespread loss of faith. On the contrary, participation in religious festivals and rituals remains robust across the country. The scattered images of discarded idols are exceptions rather than the rule and are more accurately attributed to logistical or environmental issues than to a decline in religious belief.

In summary, while the improper disposal of religious idols is an occasional issue in India, particularly after large festivals, there is no substantiated evidence that this practice signifies a mass loss of faith among Indians. The cultural context and logistical challenges surrounding idol disposal must be taken into account before drawing conclusions about the spiritual beliefs of a diverse and deeply religious society.

A video circulating widely on social media depicts a man wearing a hard hat and face mask, holding up a circuit board with the inscription “COV-19.” In the video, the man claims he is involved in installing “5G masts” and suggests a link between the circuit board, 5G technology, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The video has fueled conspiracy theories online, with many users alleging a connection between 5G network infrastructure and the spread of the coronavirus.

To assess the veracity of these claims, it is important to break down the core elements: the circuit board marked “COV-19,” the man’s purported role installing 5G equipment, and the allegations of a link between 5G technology and COVID-19.

First, the claim that 5G technology is related to the spread of COVID-19 has been widely discredited by scientists and health authorities. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which spreads primarily through respiratory droplets from person to person. 5G is a wireless communication technology that enables faster data transmission for mobile devices. There is no scientific basis or evidence to suggest that 5G technology can transmit viruses or cause the spread of COVID-19.

Second, the circuit board shown in the video with the marking “COV-19” has been scrutinized by technology experts and electronics hobbyists. Analysis of similar boards reveals that they are generic components used in televisions and other consumer electronics. The “COV-19” marking is likely a manufacturer’s internal code or batch number. Such markings are common in the electronics industry and do not indicate any link to the COVID-19 virus or to 5G equipment. In fact, the circuit board in the video does not resemble those typically used in telecommunications infrastructure, which are generally much larger and more complex than the board shown.

Third, the video’s implication that the man is installing 5G masts is unsupported by any verifiable evidence. The video provides no details about the location, context, or employer, and experts have noted that individuals involved in telecommunications installations follow strict safety and documentation protocols. The attire and setting in the video do not necessarily indicate involvement in official telecommunications work.

The video appears to be part of a broader trend of misinformation that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic. Several conspiracy theories have falsely claimed links between 5G technology and the coronavirus, leading to widespread confusion and, in some cases, vandalism of telecommunications infrastructure.

In summary, the claim that a circuit board labeled “COV-19” is part of 5G equipment and linked to the coronavirus pandemic is unfounded. The inscription is a routine manufacturing label, the board is not a component of 5G masts, and there is no scientific evidence connecting 5G technology to COVID-19. The video in question perpetuates a debunked conspiracy theory and should not be regarded as credible evidence of any link between telecommunications technology and the pandemic.

A recent social media post has gained attention for its straightforward statement: “A vaccinated bride seeks a vaccinated groom.” This post, while succinct, touches on several important themes related to COVID-19 vaccination, public health, and the ways in which the pandemic has influenced personal relationships and social expectations. This article examines the context and implications of such a statement, breaks down the core claim, and provides a fact-based analysis.

Context and Background

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccination status has become a significant factor in many aspects of daily life. Governments and health organizations around the world have promoted COVID-19 vaccines as an essential tool to reduce the spread of the virus, prevent severe illness, and protect vulnerable populations. As a result, vaccination status has increasingly influenced social dynamics, including dating and marriage.

Online dating platforms and matrimonial services have reported a rise in users specifying vaccine preferences or requirements when searching for partners. For many, vaccination status has become a proxy for shared values related to health, safety, and trust in science. Additionally, concerns about vulnerability to COVID-19, particularly among immunocompromised individuals or those with high-risk family members, have led to more people seeking partners who are also vaccinated.

Fact-Checking Analysis

The core claim of the social media post is that a bride who is vaccinated is seeking a groom who is also vaccinated. This is a personal preference and not a factual claim that can be proven true or false in the traditional sense. However, several factual components underpin the context of this preference:

1. Vaccination Status as a Criterion: It is factual that many individuals now consider vaccination status an important criterion when choosing a partner. Surveys and anecdotal reports confirm that some people are unwilling to date or marry those who are unvaccinated, citing health concerns and compatibility.

2. Vaccine Efficacy and Safety: COVID-19 vaccines have been shown to reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from the virus. Health agencies globally recommend vaccination for eligible individuals as a key measure to control the pandemic.

3. Social and Cultural Shifts: The pandemic has accelerated changes in social norms, with health status—especially regarding infectious diseases—becoming a more prominent factor in relationships. This has led to new forms of social signaling, such as specifying vaccination status in personal ads or profiles.

4. No Legal Requirement: While some businesses and venues may require proof of vaccination, there is no law mandating that individuals must marry someone of a certain vaccination status. This remains a matter of personal choice.

Conclusion

In summary, the social media post reflects a genuine trend in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic: individuals prioritizing vaccination status when seeking a partner. This preference is grounded in public health recommendations and evolving social norms. While the statement is personal and not a verifiable fact in itself, it accurately represents a widespread phenomenon in contemporary society.

Contexte et fondements

Depuis le début de la pandémie de COVID-19, le statut vaccinal est devenu un facteur important dans de nombreux aspects de la vie quotidienne. De plus, les préoccupations liées à la vulnérabilité face au COVID-19, notamment chez les personnes immunodéprimées ou celles ayant des proches à risque, ont conduit à plus de personnes cherchant des partenaires également vaccinés.

Analyse fondée sur les faits

L'affirmation centrale du message sur les réseaux sociaux est que la future épouse vaccinée cherche un futur époux également vacciné. Il s'agit d'une préférence personnelle et non d'une affirmation factuelle pouvant être vérifiée dans le sens traditionnel. Cependant, plusieurs éléments factuels sous-tendent le contexte de cette préférence :

1. Le statut vaccinal comme critère : Il est factuel que de nombreuses personnes considèrent aujourd'hui le statut vaccinal comme un critère important lors du choix d'un partenaire. Les enquêtes et les rapports anecdotiques confirment que certaines personnes sont réticentes à sortir avec ou à épouser des personnes non vaccinées, en citant des préoccupations sanitaires et une compatibilité.

2. Efficacité et sécurité des vaccins : Les vaccins contre le COVID-19 ont montré une réduction du risque de formes graves de la maladie, d'hospitalisation et de décès liés au virus. Les agences sanitaires à l'échelle mondiale recommandent la vaccination pour les personnes éligibles comme mesure clé pour contrôler la pandémie.

3. Changements sociaux et culturels : La pandémie a accéléré des changements dans les normes sociales, avec l'état de santé, notamment en ce qui concerne les maladies infectieuses, devenant un facteur plus marquant dans les relations. Cela a conduit à de nouvelles formes de signalement social, comme la spécification du statut vaccinal dans les publicités personnelles ou les profils.

Conclusion

En résumé, le message sur les réseaux sociaux reflète une tendance réelle après la pandémie de COVID-19 : les individus priorisant le statut vaccinal lors de la recherche d'un partenaire. Cette préférence s'appuie sur les recommandations en matière de santé publique et les normes sociales évoluantes. Bien que le message soit personnel et ne soit pas lui-même une affirmation vérifiable, il représente fidèlement un phénomène courant dans la société contemporaine.

In recent months, social media platforms have seen a surge of posts claiming that Covaxin, an Indian-made COVID-19 vaccine, “consists of newborn calf serum.” This assertion has sparked concern and confusion, particularly among vegetarians, vegans, and certain religious communities. Given these concerns, it is crucial to examine what Covaxin actually contains, the role of newborn calf serum in vaccine development, and whether the claim accurately represents the vaccine’s composition.

Covaxin is an inactivated virus vaccine developed by Bharat Biotech in collaboration with the Indian Council of Medical Research. It is one of the first COVID-19 vaccines developed and manufactured in India and has played a significant role in the country’s vaccination campaign.

The claim that Covaxin “consists of newborn calf serum” stems from the vaccine development process. Newborn calf serum, also known as “fetal bovine serum,” is a nutrient-rich fluid collected from the blood of calves. It is widely used in cell culture laboratories worldwide because it provides essential growth factors that help cells grow and multiply. In vaccine manufacturing, cell cultures are often used to grow viruses or bacteria that are then inactivated or weakened to create vaccines.

In the case of Covaxin, newborn calf serum is reportedly used in the initial stages of the virus cultivation process. Specifically, it is used to grow Vero cells, a type of cell line derived from the kidney of an African green monkey, which are then used to propagate the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Once the virus has been grown, it undergoes a series of inactivation and purification steps. These steps are designed to ensure that no calf serum, cells, or other unwanted materials remain in the final vaccine product. The purified, inactivated virus is then formulated with other components such as adjuvants to create the final vaccine.

Therefore, while newborn calf serum is indeed used as part of the manufacturing process, the assertion that Covaxin “consists of newborn calf serum” is misleading. The serum does not remain in the finished vaccine that is administered to people. International standards for vaccine production include strict purification processes to remove any residual animal-derived materials. Regulators require extensive quality control checks to confirm that the final vaccine is free from such impurities.

It is also important to note that the use of animal serum in vaccine development is not unique to Covaxin; many vaccines, including some produced in other countries, rely on similar cell culture techniques. The use of these materials is common practice in the biopharmaceutical industry and is considered safe by global health authorities when proper purification steps are followed.

In summary, while newborn calf serum is used in the early stages of Covaxin’s production, it is not present in the final vaccine. The claim that Covaxin “consists of newborn calf serum” misrepresents the facts and may unnecessarily alarm those considering vaccination. Understanding the vaccine’s development process can help dispel misconceptions and support informed decision-making.

در ماه‌های اخیر، پلتفرم‌های رسانه‌های اجتماعی به یک افزایش قابل توجه در پست‌هایی که ادعا می‌کنند واکسن کووکسین، یک واکسن کووید-۱۹ ساخته شده در هند، "از خون جنین گاو تشکیل شده است"، دست یافته‌اند. این ادعا باعث نگرانی و ابهام شده است، به ویژه در میان افرادی که به رژیم غذایی گیاهی یا وژان پایبند هستند و برخی جوامع دینی نیز. با توجه به این نگرانی‌ها، مطالعه این نکته ضروری است که کووکسین در واقع چه محتویاتی دارد، نقش خون جنین گاو در توسعه واکسن چیست و آیا این ادعا به درستی ترکیب واکسن را نشان می‌دهد.

کووکسین یک واکسن غیرفعال شده است که توسط شرکت بھارت بیوتک در همکاری با موسسه تحقیقات پزشی هندی ساخته شده است. این یکی از اولین واکسن‌های کووید-۱۹ که در هند توسعه و تولید شده است و در حمله اقدامات واکسیناسیون کشور نقش مهمی داشته است.

ادعای اینکه کووکسین "از خون جنین گاو تشکیل شده است" از فرآیند توسعه واکسن ناشی می‌شود. خون جنین گاو، که به نام "خون جنین گاو" نیز شناخته می‌شود، یک مایع غنی از نظر مواد مغذی است که از خون گاو‌های نوزاد جمع‌آوری می‌شود. این مایع در آزمایشگاه‌های فرهنگ سلولی جهانی به طور گسترده استفاده می‌شود زیرا این عوامل رشد ضروری را فراهم می‌کند که به رشد و تکثیر سلول‌ها کمک می‌کند. در تولید واکسن، اغلب از فرهنگ سلولی برای رشد ویروس یا باکتری استفاده می‌شود که سپس غیرفعال یا ضعیف سازی می‌شود تا واکسن تولید شود.

در مورد کووکسین، خون جنین گاو به گفته‌ها در مراحل اولیه فرآیند رشد ویروس استفاده می‌شود. به طور خاص، این خون برای رشد سلول‌های Vero، یک نوع فرهنگ سلولی که از کلیه یک مار سبز آفریقایی گرفته شده است، استفاده می‌شود. سپس این سلول‌ها برای انتشار ویروس کووید-۱۹ (SARS-CoV-2) استفاده می‌شوند. پس از رشد ویروس، این ویروس از طریق یک سری مراحل غیرفعال سازی و پاکسازی می‌گذرد. این مراحل به طور طراحی شده‌ای انجام می‌شود تا اطمینان حاصل شود که هیچ خون جنین گاو، سلول یا مواد غیرخواسته‌ای در محصول نهایی واکسن باقی نماند. سپس ویروس غیرفعال و پاک شده با مواد دیگر مانند افزاینده‌ها برای ساخت واکسن نهایی مخلوط می‌شود.

بنابراین، اگرچه خون جنین گاو در فرآیند ساخت کووکسین به طور واقعی استفاده می‌شود، ادعا اینکه "کووکسین از خون جنین گاو تشکیل شده است" اشتباه است. خون جنین گاو در محصول نهایی واکسنی که به مردم تزریق می‌شود، وجود ندارد. استانداردهای بین‌المللی تولید واکسن شامل فرآیندهای پاکسازی سختگیرانه برای حذف هرگونه مواد مشتق از حیوان است. نظارران الزام دارند از چک‌های کنترل کیفیت بسیار جزئی برای تأیید اینکه واکسن نهایی از این ایمپورت‌ها پاک باشد استفاده کنند.

همچنین مهم است توجه داشته باشیم که استفاده از خون جنین گاو در توسعه واکسن فقط در کووکسین نیست؛ بسیاری از واکسن‌ها، شامل برخی واکسن‌های ساخته شده در کشورهای دیگر نیز از فرآیندهای مشابه فرهنگ سلولی استفاده می‌کنند. استفاده از این مواد در صنعت فارماکوبیولوژی رایج است و به طور کلی توسط نهادهای سلامت جهانی به عنوان ایمن شناخته می‌شود، اگر مراحل پاکسازی مناسبی رعایت شود.

در نهایت، هر چند خون جنین گاو در مراحل اولیه ساخت کووکسین استفاده می‌شود، اما در واکسن نهایی وجود ندارد. ادعا اینکه "کووکسین از خون جنین گاو تشکیل شده است" حقیقت را نمی‌تواند نشان دهد و ممکن است افرادی که به واکسیناسیون فکر می‌کنند را ناخواسته نگران کند. درک فرآیند توسعه واکسن می‌تواند به ایجاد اشتباهات و حمایت از تصمیمات آگاهانه کمک کند.

A recent social media post has claimed that the Deccan Chronicle reported vaccine hesitancy rates as high as 74.53%. This assertion has generated significant discussion online, with many expressing concern about the implications of such a high rate of reluctance toward vaccines. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine its context, explore background information on vaccine hesitancy in India, and analyze the available evidence regarding the source and validity of the cited figure.

Vaccine hesitancy refers to the delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite the availability of vaccination services. It can be influenced by factors such as misinformation, lack of trust in health authorities, concerns about vaccine safety, religious or cultural beliefs, and previous negative experiences with healthcare systems. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine hesitancy has been a significant concern worldwide, including in India, where widespread immunization is critical to controlling outbreaks and protecting public health.

The Deccan Chronicle is a well-known English-language newspaper in India, with coverage of national and international news, including public health matters. A claim that it reported a vaccine hesitancy rate as high as 74.53% would suggest a severe challenge to vaccination efforts and would be noteworthy if accurate.

Upon reviewing recent articles and reports published by the Deccan Chronicle, there is no evidence to support the claim that the newspaper reported vaccine hesitancy at 74.53%. Historically, surveys and studies on vaccine hesitancy in India have shown a range of figures, often varying by region, age group, and the specific vaccine in question. At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, some surveys did indicate hesitancy rates as high as 30-40% in certain communities or at specific times. However, these numbers have generally declined as awareness campaigns increased and more people observed the positive impact of vaccination.

The precise figure of 74.53% is highly unusual and does not align with widely reported statistics from reputable sources or with previous coverage in the Deccan Chronicle. It is possible that this number was misinterpreted, taken out of context, or is based on a specific, isolated survey rather than a broad national assessment. In some cases, high hesitancy rates have been reported in very small communities or specific demographic groups, but not as a general figure for the larger population.

In summary, there is no verifiable evidence that the Deccan Chronicle reported vaccine hesitancy at 74.53%. The figure appears to be either a misrepresentation or a misunderstanding of a more limited or context-specific finding. While vaccine hesitancy remains a concern, the actual rates are generally lower than claimed in the post. Readers are advised to seek information from multiple reliable sources and to approach viral social media statistics with caution.

در بررسی مقالات و گزارشات اخیر منتشر شده در "دیکن چرونیکل"، هیچ شواهدی برای ادعای اینکه روزنامه نرخ ممانعت از واکسن را به 74.53 درصد اعلام کرده است، یافت نشده است. در طول تاریخ، پژوهش‌ها و سرویس‌های مرتبط با ممانعت از واکسن در هند نشان داده‌اند که اعداد مختلفی وجود دارد، معمولاً با توجه به منطقه، گروه سنی و واکسن مورد نظر متغیر است. در بالاترین پیک بیماری کووید-19، برخی از پژوهش‌ها نشان داده‌اند که در برخی جوامع یا در زمان‌های خاص نرخ ممانعت از واکسن به 30-40 درصد می‌رسید. با این حال، این اعداد به طور کلی کاهش یافته‌اند که با افزایش اطلاع‌رسانی و تأثیر مثبت واکسیناسیون در جوامع بیشتر مشاهده شده است.

عدد دقیق 74.53 درصد بسیار نادر و با شواهد گسترده از منابع معتبر یا پوشش قبلی در "دیکن چرونیکل" هم‌خوانی ندارد. احتمالاً این عدد به دلیل تفسیر نادرست، خارج از زمینه یا مبنی بر یک پژوهش خاص و جداگانه است، نه یک بررسی کلی در سطح کشور. در برخی موارد، نرخ بالای ممانعت از واکسن در جوامع بسیار کوچک یا گروه‌های دموگرافیک خاص گزارش شده است، اما به عنوان یک عدد کلی برای جمعیت بزرگ‌تر نیست.

در نهایت، هیچ شواهد قابل تأییدی وجود ندارد که "دیکن چرونیکل" نرخ ممانعت از واکسن را به 74.53 درصد اعلام کرده باشد. این عدد به نظر می‌رسد که یا نمایش نادرستی یا تفسیر اشتباهی از یافته‌های محدود یا به ویژه در یک زمینه است. هرچند ممانعت از واکسن هنوز یک نگرانی است، اما نرخ واقعی آن به طور کلی پایین‌تر از ادعای پست در شبکه‌های اجتماعی است. خوانندگان بهتر است از منابع متعدد و معتبر اطلاعات را جستجو کنند و به آمارهای اجتماعی با حذر نگاه کنند.
